title: Mapping Function From What Breaks
endLine: Lesions show a region is needed, not that it works alone.

scenes.tts: If part of the brain breaks, how do we know its job? A patient named Leborgne could hardly speak, yet much of his understanding survived. When he died, Broca found damage on the left frontal lobe. Such damage is a lesion, and studying what fails is a lesion study.
scenes.caption: If part of the brain breaks, how do we know its job? A patient named Leborgne could hardly speak, yet much of his understanding survived. When he died, Broca found damage on the left frontal lobe. Such damage is a lesion, and studying what fails is a lesion study.
scenes.visual: Schematic top-down brain and descending spinal cord fill most of the frame height on the left, with a live two-row output panel on the right (large high-contrast labels: 'Speech' and 'Understanding', plus a clean 'Schematic' tag). Slow ambient pulses drift along unbroken pathways. A dark lesion gap opens on the surface of the left frontal lobe before it is named; the Speech output dims and stalls while the Understanding pulses keep flowing cleanly. A bright label 'Left frontal lesion' highlights the gap.

scenes.visual: The same schematic brain and spinal cord soften slightly in the background while ambient pathway pulses keep moving slowly; the title 'Mapping Function From What Breaks' holds at full contrast.

scenes.tts: Lesion evidence has two sources. In patient studies, a stroke or operation damages part of the brain. In animal studies, researchers cut a route or destroy a neuron cluster, a nucleus, with electric current. Either way, compare what fails with what survives.

scenes.visual: Same schematic nervous system (tagged 'Schematic'). First, a natural irregular lesion patch fades onto one brain zone ('Patient: stroke or operation'). Next, on the same schematic, it transforms into a sharp cut across a tract and a tiny glowing cluster of dots labelled 'Nucleus' darkened by a brief electric spark ('Animal: planned lesion'). On the right output panel, one bar drops ('Fails') while the paired bar keeps pulsing steadily ('Survives').
scenes.narration: Lesion evidence has two sources. In patient studies, a stroke or operation damages part of the brain. In animal studies, researchers cut a route or destroy a neuron cluster, a nucleus, with electric current. Either way, compare what fails with what survives.

scenes.tts: Next, follow the broken route toward the body. A lesion removes signals from the fibres it cuts. Count how many midline crossings lie ahead. Each crossing flips the side. An odd count affects the opposite side. An even count keeps the same side.
scenes.caption: Next, follow the broken route toward the body. A lesion removes signals from the fibres it cuts. Count how many midline crossings lie ahead. Each crossing flips the side. An odd count affects the opposite side. An even count keeps the same side.
scenes.visual: Same schematic brain and spinal cord (tagged 'Schematic'), now showing a crisp dashed vertical midline down the centre. A glowing pathway runs from the brain down into the cord, crossing the midline once as a moving pulse travels along it. When a cut appears on the pathway, downstream pulses stop dead. A clean counter badge highlights the midline crossing ('One crossing -> opposite') and briefly shows a second crossing flipping back ('Two crossings -> same side').
scenes.narration: Next, follow the broken route toward the body. A lesion removes signals from the fibres it cuts. Count how many midline crossings lie ahead. Each crossing flips the side. An odd count affects the opposite side. An even count keeps the same side.

scenes.tts: Try that rule on movement. A stroke deep in the left hemisphere lies above one midline crossing. One is odd, so it weakens the right face, arm, and leg. Now cut the right half of the neck spinal cord, below that crossing. Which side becomes weak?

scenes.visual: Same schematic brain, dashed midline, and spinal cord (tagged 'Schematic'), with 'Left body' and 'Right body' bars at the bottom right. First, a stroke marker lights deep in the left hemisphere above the midline crossing; the signal fades downstream across the midline and dims the Right body indicator ('Left stroke -> right weakness'). Next, that stroke clears and a bright cut marker appears on the right half of the spinal cord in the neck, below the crossing. A bold question banner appears: 'Which side becomes weak?'
scenes.narration: Try that rule on movement. A stroke deep in the left hemisphere lies above one midline crossing. One is odd, so it weakens the right face, arm, and leg. Now cut the right half of the neck spinal cord, below that crossing. Which side becomes weak?

scenes.visual: Hold the schematic brain and spinal cord with the right-neck cord cut glowing below the midline crossing and the question 'Which side becomes weak?' clearly visible. Keep subtle ambient motion pulsing gently along the intact upper pathway above the cut so the frame is never frozen.

scenes.tts: The right arm and leg. The pathway already crossed above the neck, so zero crossings remain below the cut. Zero is even, so the same side. Lesions on opposite sides weaken the same limbs because both break one chain. So a deficit shows a region is a needed link, not that it works alone.
scenes.caption: The right arm and leg. The pathway already crossed above the neck, so zero crossings remain below the cut. Zero is even, so the same side. Lesions on opposite sides weaken the same limbs because both break one chain. So a deficit shows a region is a needed link, not that it works alone.
scenes.visual: Same schematic (tagged 'Schematic'): the dimmed signal runs straight down from the right-neck cut to the Right body bar ('No crossings ahead -> right side'). Briefly ghost both lesions together—left hemisphere and right neck cord—highlighting that both interrupt the same single chain to the right limbs. Then the chain pulses softly as a clean rule banner settles: 'Needed in a chain, not alone.'
scenes.narration: The right arm and leg. The pathway already crossed above the neck, so zero crossings remain below the cut. Zero is even, so the same side. Lesions on opposite sides weaken the same limbs because both break one chain. So a deficit shows a region is a needed link, not that it works alone.

scenes.tts: That is why lesions can mislead. Destroying one region also cuts fibres passing through it. And the region may be only a relay. Real strokes often break several stretches, and different lesions can give one pattern. Researchers guard against this by testing spared skills, comparing patients, and adding other tests.

scenes.visual: Same schematic brain (tagged 'Schematic'), zoomed smoothly onto one damaged node. First, two passing fibre lines threaded through the node snap along with it ('Passing fibres cut'). Next, a broad irregular stroke patch overlaps three adjacent stretches ('Several stretches broken'), and two different lesion spots map to the same dimmed output bar. Finally, three crisp check icons appear beside the output panel ('Spared skills', 'Multiple patients', 'Other tests') as ambient pulses resume.

scenes.tts: Used carefully, lesions unlocked major findings. In 1957, William Scoville and Brenda Milner described patient H M after his operation. He could almost never form lasting new declarative memories, the kind you can tell someone about. Yet practice improved his drawing, so another system kept a record. Memory is several abilities.

scenes.visual: Same schematic brain and output panel (tagged 'Schematic'), with a small tag 'Scoville and Milner, 1957'. A surgical lesion highlights deep memory routes; on the right panel, the 'New declarative memories' bar drops flat while a second parallel route stays bright and drives a rising 'Drawing practice' bar—splitting one 'Memory' label cleanly into two separate tracks.

scenes.tts: The suprachiasmatic nucleus sits just above where the optic nerves meet. In 1972, Friedrich Stephan and Irving Zucker destroyed it on both sides in albino rats. The rats still drank, but no longer on a daily schedule. That showed the nucleus is needed for timing, not that it generates time.

scenes.visual: Same schematic brain (tagged 'Schematic'), now highlighting a small paired nucleus at the base of the forebrain ('SCN, both sides') with tag 'Stephan and Zucker, 1972'. On the right panel, a schematic daily wave of drinking and movement flattens into scattered irregular ticks as both SCN dots darken, while a 'Drinking continues' bar stays active. A brief note appears: 'Needed for timing, not proof it keeps time'.

scenes.tts: In 2002, Olausson and colleagues studied a patient without the large, fast touch fibres. Stimulating slow C tactile fibres on hairy skin still gave a faint, pleasant sensation. That showed what those fibres can do without the large ones, not that they are needed. Each case compares what broke with what survived.

scenes.visual: Same schematic nervous system (tagged 'Schematic') with tag 'Olausson and colleagues, 2002'. Two parallel incoming sensory lines enter from the left: a thick fast fibre fades out ('Large fibres absent') while a thin slow fibre ('Slow C-tactile') carries a gentle pulse up into the brain, lighting a soft 'Faint pleasant sensation' output. The whole schematic then pulls back to show its connected network pulsing gently.
